newsitem.title: USA: U.S. cancer institute advises mammograms in 40s.
newsitem.headline: U.S. cancer institute advises mammograms in 40s.

text.p: The U.S. National Cancer Institute on Thursday endorsed mammograms for women in their 40s, a move that may quell four years of acrimony about the value of breast cancer screening for women under 50.

Immediately embracing recommendations issued by the institute's advisory board, NCI Director Dr. Richard Klausner said women at average risk for breast cancer should be screened every one to two years in their 40s.

Women at higher risk, such as those whose mothers or sisters had breast cancer, should consult their doctors about whether they should start mammography before age 40, and how often they should be screened in their 40s.

"We've known for quite some time that screening mammography is capable of saving lives, of reducing mortality," Klausner said. "The question that has been difficult to resolve is when women should begin regular screening mammography."
The cancer institute concluded that screening in the 40s can cut the breast cancer death rate by about 17 percent -- saving roughly 1500 to 2,000 U.S. lives a year.

At least 40 states already require health insurers to cover mammograms for women in their 40s, and Medicare does as well. President Bill Clinton said after the NCI announcement that he would try to ensure Medicare, Medicaid and federal employee health plans all follow the institute's advice.
More than 180,000 cases of breast cancer are diagnosed each year in the United States, and there are more than 40,000 deaths, mostly in women over age 50.

There has been no controversy about whether mammograms save lives among women over age 50, and the advisory board repeated its recommendation that women over that age should have mammograms every one to two years.
Until 1993, the NCI did support mammograms for women aged 40-49 but it dropped the recommendation because the data then available did not show that the testing was saving lives.
An effort to have an outside "consensus" panel reconsider the issue this year only inflamed matters because it reached no conclusions and said women should make up their own minds.

Other medical groups, including the privately funded American Cancer Society, continued to advise women under 50 to be screened. The cancer society's latest recommendation is yearly screenings, but it issued a statement backing the National Cancer Institute's "one or two year" advice, which should subdue lingering controversy.
Disputes about medical tests are not uncommon. But usually they are contained within the healthcare community.
And the breast cancer debate has become very politicized. The mammogram flap became front-page news and grist for congressional hearings, resolutions and strident complaints.

Klausner and Barbara Rimer, a Duke University cancer expert who heads the advisory panel, acknowledged they had been under pressure to come up with clearcut recommendations for women under 50. But they maintained their findings were based on science, not politics.
"We got a tremendous amount of pressure from all sides," said Klausner.

One of his harshest critics, Sen. Arlen Specter, a Pennsylvania Republican, said Thursday in a statement his Appropriations subcommittee, which controls the institute's budget, would hold more hearings into the mammogram issue.

Scientists on both sides of the issue acknowledge that the data on women under 50 is not as clear as they would like. Over 50, there is strong evidence that mammograms can cut breast cancer deaths by 30 percent.

Confusion also stems from misunderstandings over what mammograms can and cannot do. They can improve the odds but cannot guarantee survival, and they do not find all cancers, especially in younger women with denser breast tissue. And most of the suspicious lesions that mammograms do detect, especially in younger women, turn out to be harmless.

Studies have found that women often have an exaggerated view of their chances of developing breast cancer. Although the lifetime risk is one-in-eight, the risk for a woman in her 40s is one in 66 for developing breast cancer. The death rate is lower, about 29 deaths per 100,000 women in their 40s.
